episode.title: Ep. 88 — al Qaeda and Islamic State findings in new UN report

persons.name: Ayman al-Zawahiri
persons.status_detail: Killed in a US drone strike in Kabul while sheltering at a Haqqani Network safe house. The Taliban deny the death, but the guest and hosts say the US account is convincing.

mentions.quote: the second Emir of al-Qaeda, who of course was killed in a U.S. drone strike in Kabul while he was sheltering at a Haqqani network safe house
They've been putting out a series of new videos of Zawahiri... maintaining the fiction that Zawahiri is still alive

persons.name: Saif al-Adel
persons.role: De facto leader of al-Qaeda (believed successor to Zawahiri), based in Iran
persons.status_detail: UN member states' predominant view is that he is the de facto leader of al-Qaeda. He is present in Iran, and his leadership has not been publicly declared.

mentions.quote: member states' predominant view is that Saif al-Adel is now the de facto leader of al-Qaeda
Hurras al-Din receives direct instructions from Saif al-Adel
Safe, of course, has been in Iran for years

persons.name: Abu Muhammad al-Masri
persons.role: Former al-Qaeda number two and leader of al-Qaeda's Iran-based cell
persons.status_detail: Killed in Iran 'a couple years ago' (approx 2020)

mentions.quote: Previous leader of al-Qaeda in Iran... Abu Mohammed al-Musri, who was killed in Iran a couple years ago

persons.name: Abd al-Rahman al-Maghrabi
persons.role: Al-Qaeda number three, part of the Iran-based leadership cell
persons.status_detail: Described as a significant al-Qaeda leader in Iran

mentions.quote: You've also got Abd al-Rahman al-Magrabi, who is the al-Qaeda number three

persons.name: Abu Ikhlas al-Masri
persons.role: Al-Qaeda operations commander in Kunar and Nuristan
persons.status_detail: Captured by US forces in Kunar in 2010 and held for 11 years. Freed after the Taliban took Bagram in 2021, then reportedly resumed leadership, possibly reactivating Katiba Umar Farouk in Kunar and Nuristan.

mentions.quote: He was captured by U.S. forces in 2010... intermarried with Afghans
He was held for 11 years and was freed after the Taliban took control of Bagram
Katiba Umar Farouk (Red Unit) was possibly being reactivated in Kunar and Nuristan following the return of Abu Ikhlas al-Masri

persons.name: Amin al-Haq
persons.role: Osama bin Laden's former security chief
persons.status_detail: Received a Taliban parade and escort back to his home in Nangarhar within weeks of the August 2021 fall of Kabul

mentions.quote: Amin al-Haq, who was Osama bin Laden's security chief. He got a Taliban parade, a Taliban escort back to his home in Nangahar

persons.name: Abdul Haq al-Turkistani
persons.role: Leader of the Turkistan Islamic Party; member of al-Qaeda's central shura
persons.status_detail: Appeared in a video in May 2022 celebrating the Taliban victory

mentions.quote: Abdul Haq Turkestani also serves on al-Qaeda's central Shura... a U.S. State Department designation
directed from on high, from someone like Abdul Haq al-Turkistani

persons.name: Osama bin Laden
persons.status_detail: Mentioned in connection with the bin Laden documents and his security chief Amin al-Haq

mentions.quote: Osama bin Laden's security chief
we learned this from the bin Laden documents

persons.role: Senior Islamic State leader in Syria, blamed for the Hasakah prison break

aliases: Nuruddin Abdel I, Mutni (as transcribed, civil name)

persons.status_detail: Tweeted on 2023-02-20 (approx) that ISIS is the common enemy of the Taliban and the international community. The hosts criticized him for calling for cooperation with the Taliban against ISIS.

mentions.quote: Balala al-Sudani, who was this important Islamic State leader... directing money transfers to Islamic State affiliates in Central Africa and Mozambique and South Africa
he was a member of Shabab before he was turned... specially designated global terrorist in 2012
he's been in the game since 2007. He joined Shabab that year
the US did report that 10 other Islamic State Somalia members were killed alongside him

having spent five years looking at these kind of figures, I ended up feeling that they were only ever very approximate

organizations.name: al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: Leadership cell in Iran led by Saif al-Adel. It cannot publicly acknowledge Zawahiri's death because it would contradict the Taliban narrative. Its affiliates have not publicly broken ranks.

organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: Denies Zawahiri was killed in Kabul. Allows al-Qaeda figures to return and operate. Seeks ties with China, Russia and Central Asian states.

organizations.name: Haqqani Network
organizations.notes: Zawahiri was sheltering at one of its safe houses in Kabul.

organizations.name: Hurras al-Din
organizations.notes: Al-Qaeda branch in northwestern Syria. It aspires to attack the West but has financing difficulties, and receives direct instructions from Saif al-Adel per one member state. Estimated at hundreds to thousands of fighters.

organizations.name: Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps
organizations.notes: Bill Roggio assesses it monitors al-Qaeda communications from Iran.

organizations.name: Iran
organizations.notes: Hosts the al-Qaeda leadership cell and denies al-Qaeda presence. Fitton-Brown assumes the single UN member state rejecting the claims is Iran.

organizations.name: UN Security Council Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team
aliases: UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team
organizations.notes: Covers the Islamic State, al-Qaeda and the Taliban. Edmund Fitton-Brown is its former coordinator.

organizations.name: Katiba Umar Farouk
organizations.notes: Al-Qaeda-linked unit possibly being reactivated in Kunar and Nuristan under Abu Ikhlas al-Masri, per one member state. It is distinct from the Taliban's Red Unit.

organizations.name: Taliban Red Unit
organizations.notes: Taliban elite shock troops. Foreign fighters, including a German captured in 2018 and al-Qaeda fighters, have fought alongside them, notably in Panjshir.

organizations.name: Turkistan Islamic Party
organizations.notes: Uyghur group and al-Qaeda affiliate. The UN reports it worked with ISKP to target Chinese interests in Kabul. The hosts think disaffected elements are responsible, not the leadership.

organizations.name: Islamic State Khorasan Province
organizations.notes: Publishes magazines in Russian, Tajik and Uzbek. Runs a propaganda campaign against China, recruits disaffected Central Asians, and poached thousands from the TTP. It receives about $25,000 a month via crypto from the Al-Karrar office.

organizations.name: Islamic State
organizations.notes: Leadership succession handled smoothly, from Abu al-Hasan al-Hashimi al-Qurashi to Abu al-Hussein al-Qurashi. There is little command and control over African affiliates.

organizations.name: Al-Karrar office
organizations.notes: Islamic State Somalia financial and regional hub. It raises about $100,000 a month and sends about $25,000 a month to ISKP via crypto. It links ISCAP/ADF and Mozambique. Its leader Bilal al-Sudani was killed.

organizations.name: Islamic State Central Africa Province
aliases: Islamic State Central Africa Province (ISCAP) / ADF
organizations.notes: Growing stronger in the DRC. Has hardened foreign fighters and more sophisticated IEDs.

organizations.name: Islamic State Mozambique Province
organizations.notes: Weakened over the past year by regional forces and Mozambican reinforcements.

organizations.name: Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan
organizations.notes: ISKP poached thousands of its fighters. Harbored by the Afghan Taliban, which causes tension with Pakistan.

organizations.name: Jamaat Ansarullah
organizations.notes: Tajik jihadist group supported by the Turkistan Islamic Party per the UN report.

organizations.name: Pakistani military and intelligence establishment
organizations.notes: Historically supported the Afghan Taliban for strategic depth against India and tolerated TTP attacks.

organizations.name: US Central Command
organizations.notes: Announced the killing of a senior Islamic State leader responsible for the Hasakah prison break.

organizations.name: al-Shabaab
organizations.notes: Sudani was a member of Shabab before joining the Islamic State.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula
organizations.notes: Its threat was hobbled by the killing of bomb maker al-Asiri.

organizations.name: Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin
organizations.notes: Cited as an example of why one should not co-opt one extremist group against another.

organizations.name: Syrian Democratic Forces
organizations.notes: Fought the Islamic State in the Hasakah prison battle. The host calls them essentially the PKK.

organizations.name: Afghan security forces
organizations.notes: About 300,000 strong, backed by US troops, used in Bill Roggio's argument that the 75,000 Taliban estimate was too low.

organizations.name: Al-Furqan office
organizations.notes: IS regional office handling DRC/Mozambique, probably finance (Fitton-Brown); distinct from Al-Karrar (Somalia).

events.description: US drone strike kills al-Qaeda emir Ayman al-Zawahiri at a Haqqani Network safe house in Kabul.
Abu Muhammad al-Masri, al-Qaeda's number two and Iran-based leader, is killed in Iran.
US forces capture al-Qaeda operations commander Abu Ikhlas al-Masri in Kunar.
After the Taliban took Bagram, Abu Ikhlas al-Masri is freed after about 11 years in detention, along with other al-Qaeda, IS and Taliban prisoners.
Amin al-Haq returns to Nangarhar with a Taliban parade and escort within weeks of the fall of Afghanistan.
Abdul Haq al-Turkistani appears in a video celebrating the Taliban victory.
Taliban assault on Panjshir, with foreign fighters including al-Qaeda alongside the Red Unit.
Islamic State prison break at Hasakah, blamed on Ibrahim al-Katani.
CENTCOM announces it killed senior Islamic State leader Ibrahim al-Katani.
Zalmay Khalilzad tweets that cooperation with the Taliban against ISIS can be a key part of future relations.
US raid in Somalia kills Bilal al-Sudani and about 10 other Islamic State Somalia members and seizes hard drives and laptops.
Bilal al-Sudani designated a Specially Designated Global Terrorist.
Bilal al-Sudani joins al-Shabaab and becomes foreign fighter coordinator and recruiter.
UN 30th Monitoring Team report publishes findings on ISIL regional structures and the Al-Karrar office's financial hub role and funds to Afghanistan.
Suicide bombing in Goma, North Kivu, attributed to ADF-linked activity. The speaker said it took place 'last April'; it is resolved against the 2023 publish date.

sources_cited: UN Monitoring Team report (Feb 2023) on ISIL and al-Qaeda
Earlier UN Monitoring Team reports on foreign terrorist fighters in Mozambique and DRC
key_claims: ISIL affiliates in Mozambique and DRC are diverging: Mozambique is declining while ADF in DRC is growing.
The UN report repeatedly stresses the absence of ISIL command and control over affiliates; IS structures facilitate and assist rather than direct.
Affiliate operations supply fodder for ISIL's global propaganda.
The Somalia-based Al-Karrar office likely serves finance and facilitation roles for the Mozambique and DRC affiliates.
More sophisticated ADF IEDs suggest outside trainers or IS support, though member states lack direct evidence.
The 280-fighter estimate for IS Mozambique is probably too low given the scale of the conflict; absolute fighter counts are unreliable, but trends are useful.
The ADF's growth has been boosted by a large jailbreak, whose majority joined ADF.
